prompt: Which of these is a service level indicator in this lesson's sense?
hint: Good events over valid events, as customers see them.

choices.text: The average CPU of the App Service plan
choices.why: CPU is a cause; no customer feels it directly.

choices.text: Successful checkouts over all checkouts
choices.why: Right. A ratio counted from what customers received.

choices.text: The number of instances running
choices.why: A count of machines says nothing about what customers got.

choices.text: Deployments per week
choices.why: That measures delivery, not the service customers receive.

prompt: Why does the speed indicator count `Success and DurationMs <= 1000` rather than just `DurationMs <= 1000`?

choices.text: Failed requests have no DurationMs
choices.why: They do; the failed checkouts took three seconds.

choices.text: To make the indicator easier to meet
choices.why: It makes it harder, by counting fast errors as bad.

choices.text: A fast error is not a fast checkout
choices.why: Right. Without Success, quick failures would count as good.

choices.text: Kusto cannot compare a real with an integer
choices.why: It can; the reason is meaning.

prompt: What was checkout's availability on Thursday, in São Paulo's day?
At an objective of 99.5% over 29,863 checkouts, how many failures does the week's budget allow?
What makes a good objective, by this lesson's standard?
hint: Who decides when it is too low?

choices.text: The best the service has ever done
choices.why: That leaves no budget, and every release becomes a risk to it.

choices.text: 100%, so nothing is allowed to fail
choices.why: Nothing reaches 100%, and chasing it stops every release.

choices.text: The level below which customers notice
choices.why: Right. A business question, asked with data.

choices.text: Whatever the cloud provider's own SLA says
choices.why: The provider's SLA covers its services, not the shop's customers' experience.

prompt: With 19 failures of budget left, a team wants to ship a risky change on Friday. What does the error budget policy decide?

choices.text: Nothing; the policy only applies once the budget is gone
choices.why: It has a middle state for exactly this.

choices.text: It ships, and waits for a clean canary
choices.why: Right. Mostly spent means releases go on with more care.

choices.text: It is refused until next quarter
choices.why: The window is a week, and the budget is not exhausted yet.

choices.text: Whoever argues best on Friday decides
choices.why: The point of the policy is that nobody argues on the day.

prompt: At an objective of 99.5%, the error rate is 1.45% for an hour. What is the burn rate?

choices.why: That is the error rate itself.
Right. 1.45 divided by 0.5.
That divides the wrong way round.
That is the objective.

prompt: Why are alert thresholds written as burn rates rather than error rates?
hint: Think of a service at 99.9% and one at 99%.

choices.text: Burn rates are cheaper to compute in KQL
choices.why: It is one division either way.

choices.text: They put every objective on one scale
choices.why: Right. A 1% error rate is a crisis at 99.9% and normal at 99%.

choices.text: Error rates cannot be measured over an hour
choices.why: burn.kql measured them hour by hour.

choices.text: Azure Monitor accepts only burn rates in rules
choices.why: A rule's query computes whatever you write.

prompt: In two-windows.kql, why did paging stop at 17:55 although the long window still burned near 97?

choices.text: The long window's threshold rose after an hour
choices.why: The threshold is fixed at 14.4.

choices.text: The short window fell to zero
choices.why: Right. The incident was over; the hour's memory of it does not page.

choices.text: Alerts resolve automatically after 40 minutes
choices.why: Nothing here resolves by time; both windows decide.

choices.text: The budget was exhausted, so paging is pointless
choices.why: The budget was not exhausted, and that is not how the rule works.

prompt: At 18:45 the short window burned at 17.4 and nobody was paged. What does that show?
hint: What was the long window doing?

choices.text: A bug: the short window alone should page
choices.why: Both must agree, by design.

choices.text: That 18:45 was outside business hours
choices.why: Business hours are a deployment check, not part of this rule.

choices.text: The long window ignoring a blip, as it should
choices.why: Right. One failure in five minutes is not an hour of burning.

choices.text: That the threshold of 14.4 is too low
choices.why: 17.4 passed it; the long window is what held the page.

prompt: Put the moments of Thursday's incident in order, as this course's rules saw them.
hint: Start, simple rule, budget rule, recovery.
trap: Putting the burn alert first is the slip: it waits for the long window, five minutes after the simple rule.

prompt: The classic burn-rate threshold for a one-hour window, used in this lesson, is ___.
hint: A number with one decimal place.

prompt: Which statements about the shop's week are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It met its 99.5% objective
choices.why: Yes. 130 failures against 149 allowed.

choices.text: Most of the budget went in one hour
choices.why: Yes. 103 of the 130 failures fell in the 17:00 hour.

choices.text: Thursday's availability met the objective
choices.why: No. 97.4% on the day; the week met it, the day did not.

choices.text: The hour after the incident burned faster than 14.4
choices.why: No. It burned at 2.9.
